what: A data warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) stores all your company's history in columns and answers big analytics questions in SQL, scanning billions of rows in seconds.
like: Like a library archive built for research: not for checking out one book fast, but for answering 'what did everyone borrow last year?'
why: One place to join data from every app and source
Columnar storage reads only the columns a query needs
Storage and compute scale and bill separately, so you pay for queries you run

steps.d: Copy data from app databases, event streams and logs into raw tables as-is. This is ELT: load first, transform later inside the warehouse.
dbt turns raw tables into clean models using SQL SELECTs. Incremental models only process new or changed rows since the last run, saving time and money.
A fact table holds events and numbers (one row per crawler hit or citation). Dimension tables describe them (tenant, page, bot, date). Reports join facts to dimensions.
Each column is stored and compressed on its own, so a query reading 3 of 50 columns reads far less. Partitioning and clustering let it skip whole blocks.
Compute is separate from storage: BigQuery uses slots (virtual CPUs), Snowflake uses virtual warehouses that bill credits per second. Many teams can query the same data at once.

choices.d: Usually a date (event_date). Queries that filter on it skip other partitions and scan fewer bytes. Avoid tiny partitions; BigQuery suggests about 10 GB or more each.
Up to 4 columns, like tenant_id then page_id. Rows are sorted by them, so filters on tenant prune blocks. Good first step for performance.
Pay per byte scanned (on-demand) for spiky use, or reserve capacity (BigQuery slots, Snowflake warehouse size and auto-suspend) for steady, predictable spend.
Star schema for clear reports, or wide denormalised tables when joins cost more than storage. dbt incremental models for big fact tables.
Native warehouse tables are simplest. Open formats like Apache Iceberg on object storage let Spark, Trino, Flink and the warehouse share one copy.

instead.why: Sub-second dashboards on fresh events, many users clicking at once
Small data or live app reads and writes, not big scans
Lakehouse: Iceberg tables on S3, query with many engines
Results needed within seconds, computed as events arrive

breaks.d: A SELECT * over a huge table with no partition filter scans everything.
breaks.see: Bytes billed per query jumps; cost dashboard spikes
breaks.fix: Partition filters, select only needed columns, per-user quotas, dry runs

breaks.d: One big tenant's report hogs shared compute and others wait.
breaks.see: Queued queries and slot or warehouse saturation at month end
breaks.fix: Separate warehouses or reservations per workload, schedule heavy jobs

breaks.d: Hourly partitions on a small table create lots of metadata.
breaks.see: Slow planning; partition count near limits
breaks.fix: Coarser partitions (daily or monthly) plus clustering

breaks.d: Late rows are skipped or a re-run doubles rows.
breaks.see: Totals differ from a full rebuild
breaks.fix: Idempotent merges on a unique key, a look-back window, periodic full refresh

breaks.d: A nightly load fails and reports show yesterday's numbers.
breaks.see: Freshness check or max(loaded_at) older than expected
breaks.fix: dbt source freshness tests, alerts, retries in the scheduler

say: Raw crawler hits and AI citations land in BigQuery through ELT, and dbt builds a star schema: fact_hits plus tenant, page, bot and date dimensions.
The fact table is partitioned by event_date and clustered by tenant_id, so a monthly report for one tenant scans only that month and that tenant's blocks.
Monthly visibility reports for all tenants run as one scheduled job on reserved capacity, so cost is predictable instead of per-byte surprises.
Customer-facing live dashboards read from ClickHouse; the warehouse stays the source of truth for history and billing-grade reports.

followups.a: Data sits once in cheap durable storage. Compute starts, scales and stops on its own, so a month-end report can get a big cluster for an hour without paying for it all month, and teams do not block each other.

Warehouse for SQL analytics and reports with little ops. ClickHouse for sub-second, high-concurrency dashboards on fresh data. Lakehouse (Iceberg on S3) when many engines must share open data without copies.

followups.q: How do you keep multi-tenant reports safe?
followups.a: Every fact row carries tenant_id; cluster on it, and use row-level security or authorized views so a tenant's query can only see its rows. Test it in CI.
Partition and cluster, avoid SELECT *, materialise common aggregates with dbt, set quotas, and move steady workloads to reserved slots or right-sized auto-suspending warehouses.

today: Open table formats are now mainstream: Apache Iceberg tables can be read and written by Spark, Trino, Flink and others at once, and major warehouses can query them, blurring the warehouse and lakehouse line.

check.q: A report reads 3 columns from a 50-column table. Why is a warehouse fast at this?
check.a: Columnar storage reads only those 3 columns
d: It caches every row in RAM
It uses a B-tree index per row
It reads rows in parallel from the app DB
check.why: Each column is stored separately, so unused columns are never read or billed.

check.q: In a star schema, where does 'one row per crawler hit' belong?
d: In the raw landing zone only
check.why: Facts hold events and measures; dimensions describe them (tenant, page, bot, date).

check.q: Your BigQuery query filters on event_date and tenant_id. What setup cuts bytes scanned most?
check.a: Partition by event_date, cluster by tenant_id
d: Partition by tenant_id, cluster by nothing
check.why: Partitions skip other dates and clustering prunes blocks for other tenants. LIMIT does not reduce bytes scanned.

check.q: What does ELT mean compared with ETL?
check.a: Load raw data first, transform inside the warehouse
d: Transform on a separate server before loading
Export data out of the warehouse to transform
Load only data that was already cleaned
check.why: The warehouse's compute does the transforms, often with dbt, and raw data stays for re-runs.
